Chain of command, one line item each

WhoRoleFromToWhat they did
The campusesfirst responders19651970First teach-in at Michigan (24 Mar 1965); SDS march on Washington (Apr 1965); draft-card burnings; Columbia (1968); after Cambodia, a strike of some four million students, and Kent State (4 May 1970) and Jackson State (15 May 1970).
The pressthe turn19681971Cronkite's 'mired in stalemate' broadcast (27 Feb 1968); My Lai reported by Seymour Hersh (Nov 1969); the Pentagon Papers published by the Times and the Post (Jun 1971), upheld by the Supreme Court in seventeen days.
The veteransthe witnesses19671971Vietnam Veterans Against the War founded (1967); Winter Soldier hearings in Detroit (Jan–Feb 1971); Dewey Canyon III, medals thrown over the Capitol fence, and John Kerry before the Senate (Apr 1971).
The Congressthe law19701974Repealed the Gulf of Tonkin resolution (Jan 1971); Case–Church amendment cutting off funds for combat (Jun 1973); War Powers Resolution over Nixon's veto (Nov 1973); refused Ford's aid request (Apr 1975).
The armythe institution19731991Ended the draft (Jan 1973) for an all-volunteer force; rebuilt doctrine around decisive force and clear objectives, later called the Weinberger–Powell doctrine; stopped using body counts as a metric.
Hanoithe other response19681975Tet was a military defeat and a political response that worked; the Easter Offensive (1972) tested Vietnamization; the Ho Chi Minh Campaign (1975) answered the ceasefire.
The country, afterwardsthe memory19791982PTSD entered the DSM-III (1980), pushed by veterans' groups; the Vietnam Veterans Memorial, a black wall with 58,000 names and no figures, dedicated 13 Nov 1982.

Phases

1965–1967
Teach-in

Objection is academic and religious; the draft makes it personal; support for the war still holds a majority.

1968–1969
The turn

Tet, Cronkite, Johnson withdraws (31 Mar 1968), Chicago convention; a majority now calls the war a mistake; the Moratorium (15 Oct 1969) is the largest protest to date.

1970–1971
Rupture

Cambodia, Kent State, the student strike, Winter Soldier, the Pentagon Papers, the May Day arrests (12,000 in three days).

1973–1982
Settlement

Draft ends; War Powers; POWs return; Saigon falls; the country argues about the veterans and then builds them a wall.

Outcome

The war ended the draft, the president's unilateral war power on paper, the press's deference, and the metric of the body count. It did not end the war; Hanoi did that.

Open questions

  • Whether the protests shortened the war or, by hardening the 'silent majority', lengthened it — Nixon's own view was that they made withdrawal harder.
  • Whether Tet changed opinion or merely confirmed a decline already under way since 1967 in the polls.
  • Whether the all-volunteer force made later wars easier to start because fewer families had a stake.
